title: Exploring AI pilots to autonomous banking: How tech is reshaping the future of financial services
excerpt: Artificial Intelligence. 4 min read. Exploring AI pilots to autonomous banking: How tech is reshaping the future of financial services. Banks are moving towards integrating artificial intelligence into their operations and governance models. This shift aims to create an autonomous banking environment which enhances efficiency and decision-making. Significant challenges remain, including overcoming legacy architecture and ensuring proper governance frameworks are established. Financial institutions must focus on combining proprietary data and domain expertise to fully utilize AI technology. Successful implementation will differentiate leaders from laggards in the evolving banking landscape. S. Srinivasan Seshadri. ETCIO. Published On Nov 9, 2026 at 08:13 AM IST. Read by 1089 Professionals. Set ETCIO as your preferred source on Google. Copy Link. Share on WhatsApp. Share on Linkedin. Share on X. Share on Telegram. Share on Facebook. AI has quickly moved from experimentation to the boardroom, but the tougher task now is turning this momentum into an operating model that can scale safely and create lasting advantage. Getting an AI use case from a compelling demo into production in a regulated, legacy-heavy bank is rarely a model problem. Most of the time it comes down to engineering, data, integration and how the operating model is set up. The opportunity is therefore less about proving that AI works and more about redesigning how banks work. That means shifting toward ‘ autonomous banking ’ - intelligence embedded across customer engagement, operations, engineering and governance. The building blocks are available to everyone now; differentiation comes from how banks connect them. Advt. From AI pilots to the AI-native bank The first wave of AI proved the technology works with banks running pilots, copilots becoming real products and AI landing on the board agenda. But what has not happened yet is any fundamental change in how a bank operates. Half of the world's 50 largest banks now disclose active AI use cases , roughly double the previous year. But only seven report projected returns and just four report realised ROI. About 85% of generative AI deployments are still internally focused, and agentic AI is in pilot or production at only ten of the top fifty. The barriers are far more practical including enterprise data, legacy architecture, governance, and organisational readiness. These determine whether AI ever gets past the proof of concept. Operations are especially important with roughly 50 to 60% of a bank's workforce sitting there. Industrializing AI across that could create a very different economic model. And nobody has done it yet. From general-purpose AI to defensible domain intelligence Getting things ‘mostly right’ should never be good enough. A hallucinated number in a credit memo or a regulatory filing is never a quality issue, it is an incident. In such a scenario banking AI has to understand decisions, not just conversations. A credit approval or a sanctions decision carries policy, regulation, customer context and decades of institutional judgement, and no foundation model arrives with that context, however capable it is. Which is why domain knowledge is becoming increasingly important. The advantage sits in combining the model with the bank's own data, policies and workflows. Advt. And underneath all of it sits a strategic question: where does differentiation come from once AI is available to everyone? If every bank uses the same frontier model in roughly the same way, the model is not an advantage. Domain AI lets a bank build something specific to its own business and a decision can explain and defend in front of a regulator. title: Finda Launches First Open Recruitment Drive Since Savings Bank Launch... "Designing an AI-Native Bank"
excerpt: Finda Launches First Open Recruitment Drive Since Savings Bank Launch. "Designing an AI-Native Bank". by Moon Chaeseok. Published 09 Nov. 2026 09:07(KST). Share Language Text Size Print. 19 Roles in Product, Technology, Security, Compliance, and Business Support. Fintech company Finda said it will launch an open recruitment drive on November 9 for 19 roles to bring in talent to lead the savings bank it recently acquired. View original image. This is Finda's first group-wide open recruitment drive since acquiring the savings bank. The company plans to recruit talent to strengthen the business foundations of its loan comparison platform and savings bank, while redesigning its financial services and operating systems around artificial intelligence (AI). The goal of the recruitment drive is to design an "AI-native bank" that builds a new financial operating model in which AI agents and people collaborate, each drawing on their respective strengths, and focuses on creating value for financial consumers. Finda plans to redesign its products, ways of working, and overall operating systems so that AI agents handle repetitive tasks and analysis, while employees focus on decisions requiring judgment and accountability. The five recruitment areas include product and technology, security and privacy, and compliance and legal affairs. At the savings bank acquired by Finda, the company is focusing on recruiting key talent to build AI-powered financial services and an innovative banking operating system. Key positions include compliance officer, AI engineer, infrastructure engineer, security engineer, data engineer, product engineer, product owner, product designer, privacy officer, legal affairs specialist, business support specialist, and financial accounting specialist. Finda is also hiring for a range of roles, including marketing and business development, to strengthen its platform competitiveness and maximize synergies with its banking business. Applications will be accepted through November 23. Applicants may apply for multiple positions, and Finda also offers a flexible hiring process in which it recommends roles suited to candidates' experience and capabilities. The process consists of a resume screening, a job interview, and a culture-fit interview. Finda is also offering benefits to candidates who join quickly. Applicants who start within four weeks of receiving an offer letter will receive a signing bonus. For more information about each position, including job descriptions and how to apply, visit the "Careers" page in the upper-right corner of Finda's official website. Lee Hyemin, CEO of Finda, said, "This recruitment drive is not simply about creating new financial services. It is a search for colleagues who will change how traditional finance works and transform the customer experience itself. We are looking for people who challenge conventions rather than settle for established ways of doing things, create new possibilities, and, above all, remain tenaciously focused on benefits that financial consumers can actually enjoy. title: Anthropic Launches Personal Finance In Claude To Connect Bank Accounts And Analyze Spending
excerpt: . Anthropic Launches Personal Finance In Claude To Connect Bank Accounts And Analyze Spending. Anthropic has introduced Personal Finance in Claude, a new feature that allows users to connect their bank accounts, credit cards, loans, and investment accounts to its AI assistant for personalized financial analysis. The service uses Plaid to securely connect financial institutions and provides a centralized dashboard for monitoring account balances, spending patterns, cash flow, subscriptions, and upcoming bills. The feature is currently available in beta to eligible Claude Pro, Max, and Ultra subscribers in the United States. It is being introduced gradually across Claude’s web application, desktop software, and mobile apps for iOS and Android. Personal Finance is not available to users on Claude’s Free, Team, or Enterprise plans. The launch represents an expansion of Claude’s capabilities into personal financial management, allowing users to analyze information from their own financial accounts through natural-language conversations. Rather than manually reviewing transactions across different banking applications, users can ask Claude questions about their spending and financial activity. For example, customers can ask how much they spent during the previous month, identify recurring subscription payments, or examine patterns across their connected accounts. The Personal Finance dashboard includes customizable widgets showing spending, cash flow, account balances, subscriptions, upcoming bills, and AI-generated financial insights. Users can add, remove, edit, and rearrange these widgets to create a personalized overview of their finances. To connect financial accounts, customers authorize access through Plaid, a financial data connectivity platform that allows applications to retrieve account information from participating institutions. Plaid handles the bank authentication process, meaning users do not provide their banking passwords directly to Claude. Customers can connect up to 16 banks and choose which accounts they want to share. For authorized accounts, Claude can access bank and account names, account types, balances, credit limits, and up to 24 months of transaction history. Transaction details may include purchase amounts, dates, merchant names, spending categories, and descriptions provided by financial institutions. Although the feature supports connections to investment, loan, and credit card accounts, its access to these products is currently limited. Claude can retrieve balances and credit limits but cannot read individual investment holdings, trades, loan interest rates, or contractual terms. The service is also read-only and cannot transfer money, manage accounts, execute investments, or initiate financial transactions. Anthropic has incorporated privacy controls designed to give users greater visibility into how their financial data is accessed and used. Conversations conducted within the Personal Finance hub are not used to train Claude’s AI models. Financial information shared outside the hub is subject to the user’s applicable privacy settings. Customers can also disable Plaid access for regular conversations and unlink financial institutions when they no longer want Claude to retrieve their account information. Anthropic notes that financial information may not always be current. Account balances can be one or two days old, while some transactions may require additional time to synchronize. The company also cautions that AI-generated financial analyses may contain mistakes and recommends checking important figures against original bank records. Personal Finance is intended to help users understand their financial activity rather than provide investment advice. Additional limitations include support for U. S. banks only and restrictions preventing linked financial account data from being used in scheduled tasks, Claude Cowork, and Claude Code. title: Agentic AI Could Trigger a Deposit Exodus. What Banks Can Do About It
Kiwi Bank looks to AI to move faster in battle with banking behemoths
excerpt: For Kiwi Bank CEO Steve Jurkovich, the question when it comes to AI, is not whether it will change banking, but what role it will play in shaping the future of the sector. “Most importantly for us, how do we use [AI] in a way that’s absolutely aligned to our purpose, that helps us deliver for our customers and for our team, and of course for Aotearoa,” he told attendees at the recent AWS Cloud and AI conference in Auckland. “For us, that means that AI has to be at the absolute heart and be a real important part of our strategy. ”. As it’s owned by all New Zealanders, Kiwi Bank aims to drive more competition in the local market dominated by four Australian-owned banks and set itself an ambitious goal – to double its impact by 2030. That means it needs to reach more customers, support more businesses and help more Kiwis to achieve their goals, said Jurkovich. “We’ve got a long way to go until we’re as big as our big four Australian competitors. So, we’ve got to think about how we get you a deal that makes you better off,” he added. “We’re doing that really well, but we’ve also got to do it in a faster way than we’ve ever done it before. ”. As such, Jurkovich believes at its heart, AI is “absolutely not” a technology project. “It has to be a business capability,” he said. “It’s the number one thing I think in the next five years that can help us be a better bank … that is way more productive, way faster [and] that can be much better at customer experiences. Most of all, a bank that gives time back to our people [and] frees them up to think. ”. Overall, AI tools are helping Kiwi Bank move faster and provide its people with the information they need to deliver better outcomes quicker and to work quicker and easier. “We are definitely seeing that we can move faster, whether that’s in our core technology projects [or] about the service that’s showing up better every day because we can find the right information,” said Jurkovich. “For me, that is what doubling our impact is about – not only for our customers, but for us. It gives [us] an opportunity to grow faster, serve customers better, and really does play at the heart of that idea of doubling our impact by 2030. ”. Customisable products for customers. Kiwi Bank also plans to explore how AI tools can enable it to develop customisable products for customers. “For all the years I’ve been in banking, customers have always told us the same thing: ‘Know me, understand me, and offer me products that are timely and relevant. ’ AI is tailor-made to be able to produce that,” Jurkovich said. Kiwi Bank’s approach to AI has been about supporting and amplifying human expertise. “What we’re seeing is that teams can make better decisions where the grind is being done in the background and surfacing it so you can make and exercise your judgement, your human skills, your expertise – that’s really making a difference,” Jurkovich explained. The bank’s use of AI to date has been focused on removing repetitive work. It is using AI tools for call transcription and summarisation, as well as internal agents to support its operational teams, and is thinking about how to change some processes. In delivery, the bank is seeing massive uplifts across all of its development areas and with its partners. “We are seeing a shift in the way that we can move data. That’s absolutely unprecedented in the eight years I’ve been at Kiwi Bank,” Jurkovich said. “That is the promise of AI and partnering coming to life – I can see it and touch it and it’s in our P&L [profit and loss statements]. And if you’re working on it, I’d be challenging you to ask yourself, where am I seeing that in the hard metrics?”

rules.useCaseEvidence: It is using AI tools for call transcription and summarisation, as well as internal agents to support its operational teams, and is thinking about how to change some processes.
